paper_title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing approaches obtain denser credit via learned critics, process reward models, or on-policy distillation, but they rely on a value network, step-level annotations, or a stronger external teacher that increase training complexity. Meanwhile, importance sampling and clipping mitigate policy drift, but they do not specify a finite target that stops sequential updates from overshooting. In this work, we introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, TreeOPSD branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the policy-gradient direction as the tangent at the behavior policy while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. Empirically, TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across several competitive benchmarks and model scales, especially for long-horizon tasks, e.g., raising the average accuracy of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 by 4.97 points over GRPO on the Deep Research setting.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025) has emerged as central post-training paradigm for large language models (LLMs), using outcome rewards to incentivize reasoning or environment interactions on complex problem-solving tasks. While reasoning-oriented RLVR typically learns from Chain-of-Thought (CoT) rollouts, agentic RL (Yao et al., 2022) extends this paradigm to long-horizon, multi-turn trajectories in which reasoning is interleaved with actions and environment observations. As the interaction horizon grows, single terminal reward provides increasingly sparse and high-variance supervision across intermediate turns: broadcasting one trajectory-level advantage over the entire rollout over-credits unhelpful actions in successful trajectories and penalizes useful steps in failed ones (Arjona-Medina et al., 2019; Li et al., 2026a). At the same time, updating the policy across sequential mini-batches within each rollout batch induces policy staleness as the current policy departs from the behavior policy (Zheng et al., 2025a). To address the credit assignment problem, actorcritic methods such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017) estimate token-level advantages with learned critic, which is difficult to train accurately and susceptible to value flattening (Li et al., 2026c). Process reward models (PRMs) (Lightman et al., 2024) provide step-level rewards but require process annotations, and summing them as discounted returns is vulnerable to reward hacking (Cheng et al., 2026). On-policy distillation (OPD) (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024) provides dense token-level supervision on 1 student rollouts at the cost of querying stronger external teacher. Extending OPD, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026; Kaur et al., 2026) constructs self-teacher by conditioning the model on privileged context (e.g., reference solutions), which relies on task-specific heuristics and can yield unstable supervision. These limitations leave open how to derive dense intermediate credit directly from terminal verifier rewards. Sampling independent trajectories confounds all turns along each rollout, whereas multi-turn interaction exposes discrete turn-level prefixes as natural branching points. Branching alternative continuations from shared prefix fixes the preceding history to isolate how subsequent decisions affect terminal outcomes, forming rollout tree on which recursive backup converts terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit without auxiliary value or reward models (Ji et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026a). Sequential mini-batch updates on fixed rollout batch create separate optimization challenge. While all rollouts in the batch are sampled from frozen behavior policy 𝜋 𝜃old, each update step moves the current policy 𝜋 𝜃 further away, increasing policy staleness for subsequent mini-batches. Policy-gradient methods compensate for this mismatch with importance-sampling ratios, and stabilize training through clipping (Schulman et al., 2017) or ratio regularizers (Zheng et al., 2025a) as those ratios depart from one. However, such controls only constrain the importance ratio while keeping the collection-time credit fixed, so the surrogate still specifies an ascent direction rather than finite destination (Qu et al., 2026a). We therefore seek an objective that maps tree credit to finite target and adapts its gradient as 𝜋 𝜃 evolves, halting at the target and reversing sign after overshoot. Figure 1 Target construction: terminal rewards at the blooming (successful) and withered (failed) branch tips are backed up through shared prefixes to define frozen turn-level teacher along the luminous green path. Distribution matching: starting from the behavior-policy rollout (purple trail), the student policy progressively aligns with this outcome-derived target through posterior distillation. To this end, we introduce TreeOPSD, critic-free posterior selfdistillation framework for long-horizon agentic RL. TreeOPSD first maps backed-up turn credit into frozen turn-level teacher distribution relative to the behavior policy, and then minimizes the divergence between this teacher and the current student policy across sequential mini-batches. Geometrically, the tangent of this distillation objective at the behavior policy recovers the exact tree policy-gradient direction, while later mini-batches scale each update by the current studentteacher gap rather than fixed collection-time credit weight. Figure 1 illustrates this decoupling of target construction and distribution matching. In summary, our main contributions are two-fold: 1. We derive closed-form, bounded turn-level target distributions via an affine map of backed-up credit relative to the frozen behavior policy. Because this affine map commutes with tree backup, matching the backed-up parent target is gradient-equivalent to aggregating descendant distillation losses. 2. We formulate Forward-KL posterior distillation objective whose tangent at the behavior policy recovers the tree policy gradient, while its studentteacher residual vanishes at the target and reverses sign upon overshoot to stabilize sequential mini-batch optimization. Empirically, TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across competitive benchmarks and model scales, and it elicits longer-horizon agent behavior with more interaction turns in Deep Research.

sections.content: 𝑥 While the tree policy gradient 𝑔tree in Eq. 6 is exact at the on-policy point 𝜋 𝜃 = 𝜋 𝜃old, practical RLVR training partitions each rollout batch into sequential mini-batches. Once earlier mini-batches update 𝜃, the current policy 𝜋 𝜃 drifts away from the behavior policy 𝜋 𝜃old that generated the tree. Continuing to apply the collection-time credit 𝑉𝑖 as fixed linear weight ignores this off-policy drift and specifies only an initial ascent direction rather than finite destination (Qu et al., 2026a). Conversely, multiplying token gradients by raw importance ratios 𝜋 𝜃 /𝜋 𝜃old amplifies variance on long turns (Ionides, 2008; Liu et al., 2018, 2020), while ratio clipping truncates the update without defining target distribution where optimization should converge (Schulman et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2025a; Qu et al., 2026a). These limitations arise because linear policy-gradient surrogates entangle credit assignment with policy updating instead of specifying an explicit target distribution. Drawing on Policy Mirror Descent (PMD) and variational policy optimization (Beck & Teboulle, 2003; Abdolmaleki et al., 2018; Vaswani et al., 2022; Qu et al., 2026a), we decouple each iteration into two steps: first solve KL-regularized proximal improvement problem around 𝜋 𝜃old to convert backed-up turn credits into frozen target distribution, and then project the evolving policy 𝜋 𝜃 onto that target across sequential mini-batches. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented TreeOPSD, critic-free posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic RLVR. It backs sparse terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit on shared-prefix tree and mitigates policy drift by matching finite behavior-relative teacher with Forward KL. The affine target commutes with tree backup, and the distillation gradient recovers tree policy gradient at the behavior policy, then stops or reverses after overshoot, so rollout batch supports sequential updates without learned critic, process labels, or an external teacher. TreeOPSD improves over matched-budget baselines at both scales on Multi-Hop QA and Deep Research, and the gain is much larger on the longer-horizon setting.

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: RLVR and agentic RLVR. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026) trains language models from automatically checked outcomes and has produced strong reasoning policies in mathematics, coding, and other rule-based tasks. PPO remains general policy-gradient backbone (Schulman et al., 2017), while GRPO removes the learned value model by estimating advantages from response groups (Shao et al., 2024). Later variants alter the granularity of importance weighting (Zheng et al., 2025b) or organize comparisons within larger groups (Feng et al., 2025). RLVR has also moved from complete reasoning responses to agents that interleave language, tools, and environment observations (Yao et al., 2022). In this setting, single terminal advantage supervises sequence of search queries, tool calls, and answer decisions (Jin et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025d; Dong et al., 2026). TreeOPSD focuses on this turn-structured regime and derives intermediate targets directly from verifiable outcomes rather than introducing learned critic or process labels. Tree search and tree-based policy optimization. Tree search lets language models compare continuations from shared history instead of drawing only independent complete trajectories. At inference time, Tree-of-Thought (Yao et al., 2023), language-agent search (Zhou et al., 2023), and MCTS-style procedures (Feng et al., 2023) use branching to improve planning or answer selection. Offline methods turn reasoning trees into supervised or preference data (Lai et al., 2024), while online methods bring the tree into RL for exploration, value estimation, local comparisons, or rollout allocation (Hou et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025b; Zong et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026a). These approaches differ in where branches are collected and how sibling outcomes become gradients. TreeOPSD takes shared-prefix tree as input, backs terminal evidence into turn credit, and converts that credit into finite target for the current policy. Its contribution lies in optimizing the acquired tree rather than choosing where the tree should branch. Sample-eﬃcient RLVR and rollout allocation. parallel line of work reduces rollout cost by deciding which examples receive sampling budget. Offline curation fixes the training set before optimization (Ye et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025). Online methods filter prompts whose rollouts are uninformative (Yu et al., 2026; Bae et al., 2026) or predict prompt difficulty before sampling (Zheng et al., 2025c; Qu et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2026a; Qu et al., 2026b), much as automated model evaluation predicts test accuracy from unlabeled data (Peng et al., 2024). POPO replays effective groups from earlier policies in place of zero-variance groups (Mao et al., 2026b), and budget allocation varies the number of rollouts per prompt (Li et al., 2025b; Yao et al., 2026). In supervised fine-tuning, online batch selection scores samples by utility and diversity (Zou et al., 2025a). TRACE extends allocation from prompt roots to turn-level prefixes with shared success predictor (Zou et al., 2026a). These methods decide which rollouts to acquire, and TreeOPSD decides how an acquired tree updates the policy, so the two compose without changing the teacher in Section 3.2. Credit assignment under sparse rewards. Credit assignment under delayed rewards is long-standing RL problem. Temporal-difference learning (Sutton et al., 1998), potential-based shaping (Ng et al., 1999), and return decomposition (Arjona-Medina et al., 2019) provide denser signals by estimating state values or redistributing terminal returns. For language-model reasoning, process supervision and process reward models score intermediate steps (Uesato et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024), and recent work derives progress signals from Monte Carlo continuations, answer likelihoods, or implicit process objectives (Setlur et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2024). Long-horizon LLM methods further use trajectory graphs (Li et al., 2026a), vine-style continuations (Kazemnejad et al., 2025), or alternative reward aggregation (Cheng et al., 2026) to localize responsibility within rollout. Rollout trees (Ji et al., 2026; Zong et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025b) provide related source of counterfactual evidence because sibling suffixes keep the prefix fixed while varying the future. TreeOPSD backs this evidence through the sampled tree and preserves value shared by multiple useful continuations instead of removing it through sibling centering. Behavior-relative targets and posterior distillation. KL-regularized RL (Ouyang et al., 2022), maximum-aposteriori policy optimization (Abdolmaleki et al., 2018), and preference optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023; Meng et al., 2024) improve policy while anchoring it to reference distribution. Mirror-descent and mirror-ascent analyses make the corresponding target-and-projection structure explicit (Beck & Teboulle, 2003; Vaswani et al., 2022; Asad et al., 2025), and recent work applies this view to group-based language-model updates on finite response sets (Qu et al., 2026a). On-policy distillation instead trains on student-generated samples using teacher distribution (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2026; Kaur et al., 2026) or privileged continuation information (Nguyen et al., 2026). TreeOPSD joins these perspectives at the turn level. It represents each observed turn by behavior-relative Bernoulli, related to relative density-ratio estimation (Yamada et al., 2013; Cranmer et al., 2015) and contrastive source classification (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2024), then obtains closed-form teacher from backed-up credit and matches it with Forward KL. Independent turn targets avoid treating sparse sibling sample as closed continuation simplex, while the finite teacher supplies destination that fixed-credit policy gradients do not specify.

sections.title: C Discussion
sections.content: C.1 Tree acquisition, credit assignment, and policy optimization Tree-based agent RL involves three decisions that are often coupled in one algorithm. rollout procedure first decides which prompts or prefixes receive continuations. credit-assignment rule then maps terminal outcomes on that tree to turn values. Policy optimization uses those values to update the current LLM. TreeOPSD handles the last step: it takes sampled tree and normalized child weights, converts the backed-up values into behavior-relative targets, and matches the current policy to those targets. The same target construction can be paired with random branching, learned rollout allocation, or other tree samplers. C.2 Independent turn targets and pairwise preferences categorical distribution over sampled siblings is invariant to common shift of their logits or rewards. It can rank the observed continuations, but it removes value shared by all of them. This is appropriate when the sampled set is treated as closed choice set. In an LLM, however, few sampled siblings cover only small part of the continuation space. If every observed sibling is useful relative to the behavior policy, sibling-normalized update cannot raise them together. TreeOPSD instead assigns each observed turn its own behavior-relative Bernoulli target, allowing the shared policy to increase all useful turns while retaining their relative differences. Each target describes where one observed turn should move relative to its behavior likelihood. These targets do not form normalized action distribution over the full vocabulary or continuation space. Step-level preference optimization is boundary case. For two siblings with centered credits 𝑉+ = 𝑣 and 𝑉 = 𝑣, the TreeOPSD behavior-policy tangent is proportional to the usual pairwise direction log 𝜋(𝑎+) log 𝜋(𝑎). The objectives differ after that initial point. hard pairwise preference keeps enlarging the preferred margin, whereas TreeOPSD assigns both turns finite soft targets and stops when those targets are reached. When the pair has nonzero mean credit, TreeOPSD also retains the common update that pairwise centering removes. C.3 Finite-target feedback under sequential optimization Rollout batches are generated by frozen behavior policy, but later optimizer blocks run after earlier blocks have already changed the shared LLM parameters. fixed-credit surrogate continues to apply the collection-time coefficient 𝑉𝑖 even when the likelihood of turn 𝑖 has already moved. TreeOPSD keeps the teacher fixed and recomputes the student probability, replacing 𝑉𝑖 by the residual Γ𝑖 = 𝜏(𝑞𝑖 𝑝 𝜃 ,𝑖). The first block therefore follows the tree-policy-gradient tangent. Later blocks reduce, stop, or reverse the update according to the current studentteacher gap. This feedback differs from importance-ratio clipping. Clipping limits how strongly sampled action can move, but it does not specify destination. The TreeOPSD teacher supplies that destination in behavior-relative coordinate. The 21 radius 𝜌 bounds the target probability and, with it, the geometric-mean likelihood ratio of the observed turn. It sets the finite target that later blocks pursue after updates on other prompts have already moved the shared policy. C.4 Limitations and future work Allocation-aware teachers. Theorems 1 and 2 condition on the sampled tree, so TreeOPSD can train on trees from learned allocators such as DPS (Mao et al., 2026a), GPS (Qu et al., 2026b), and TRACE (Zou et al., 2026a), while its teachers still come only from verifier outcomes and behavior likelihoods. The allocator also sets the scale of those 𝐾 1 teachers. Under the Samuelson calibration, the root-mean-square of 𝑞𝑖𝑘 1/2 over the 𝐾 leaves equals 𝜌/ whenever the rewards are not all equal, about 0.075 at the default 𝜌 = 0.25 and 𝐾 = 12, and only tree with single dissenting reward reaches the full radius. Allocators that favor mixed outcomes move trees toward balanced rewards, and budget allocators vary 𝐾 across prompts (Li et al., 2025b; Yao et al., 2026). radius set from the realized credits or from 𝐾 would let allocation and teacher scale be designed together. It keeps both theorems, since the first-block tangent does not depend on 𝜏 and Theorem 1 only needs every 𝑞𝑖 in (0, 1). Tree replay. Each tree currently serves 𝐸 = 4 optimizer blocks before it is discarded. POPO saves rollouts by replaying effective groups from earlier policies in place of zero-variance groups (Mao et al., 2026b), and the same replay fits TreeOPSD. target ratio 𝑟 is defined relative to the policy that collected its tree, so replayed teacher still 𝑖 satisfies Eq. 12, and the residual 𝜏(𝑞𝑖 𝑝 𝜃 ,𝑖) shrinks or reverses on turns that the current policy has already moved toward or past their targets. The residual also scores stored turns with one forward pass, which could drive utilityand diversity-aware batch selection over replay buffer (Zou et al., 2025a). Since each 𝑉𝑖 averages continuations from the collecting policy, replayed credit ages as the policy improves, and weighting stored trees by their off-policiness, as POPO does for groups, would account for this aging. Continual agentic post-training. tree whose rewards all coincide has 𝑞𝑖 = 1/2 at every turn, so in later blocks it pulls its own turns back toward 𝜋 𝜃old, much as Learning without Forgetting distills the previous models outputs (Li & Hoiem, 2017). On-policy RL forgets less than SFT, and its forgetting tracks the KL shift on the new task (Shenfeld et al., 2026). TreeOPSD shares the on-policy sampling behind this result, and its teachers also stay within 𝜌 of 1/2. RL post-training still forgets across task sequences, however, because KL measured on current-task data does not control drift on prior-task distributions (Luo et al., 2026). Mixing few stored trees from earlier environments, together with their logged behavior probabilities, into later batches would extend the 𝑞𝑖 = 1/2 anchor to prior tasks without new rollouts. On the parameterization side, continual-learning methods mitigate the stabilityplasticity dilemma through parameter regularization (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017), fly-olfactory-circuit designs (Zou et al., 2025b, 2026b), and guided random projections (Li et al., 2026b). FlyLoRA limits inter-task interference in LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) by using frozen sparse random projection as an implicit router over rank-wise experts (Zou et al., 2025c), and TreeOPSD applies to such parameterizations unchanged because it only reweights token log-likelihood gradients. The residual already accounts for drift among prompts within batch (Appendix C.3), and decorrelated parameterization would limit interference across environments that never share batch.

These centered credits average to zero under the backup weights, so listwise cannot raise both children relative to the behavior policy. Panel (c) keeps 𝑉𝑐 and changes the teacher map. Early useful actions in an unsuccessful rollout receive the same trajectory-level signal as the eventual error, whereas branches from shared prefix show whether the next turn improves the downstream trajectory. sections.title: E Experimental and implementation details
sections.content: We follow Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025; Zou et al., 2026a) for Multi-Hop QA and OpenResearcher (Li et al., 2026d; Tao et al., 2026) for Deep Research. E.1 Datasets, environments, and rewards E.1.1 Multi-Hop QA Training data and environment. We use all 90,447 questions from the HotpotQA distractor training split (Yang et al., 2018). The agent searches local E5 retrieval server (Wang et al., 2022) built over Wikipedia dump (Karpukhin et al., 2020). Each tool call accepts up to four queries and returns the top three passages for each query. We cap rollout at five assistant turns, including the final answer, which leaves at most four tool-calling turns. Evaluation benchmarks. We evaluate on the 7,405-question HotpotQA validation split, the 12,576-question 2WikiMultiHopQA development split (Ho et al., 2020), the 2,417-question MuSiQue development split (Trivedi et al., 2022), and all 125 Bamboogle test questions (Press et al., 2023). Reward function. Training uses thresholded token F1. parsed answer receives its token-level F1 when that score is at least 0.3 and receives zero otherwise. Validation records both F1 and exact match. Table 1 and the training curves use exact match (EM). E.1.2 Deep Research Training data and environment. OpenResearcher provides 16 synthesized trajectories for each of 6,102 MiroVerse questions (Li et al., 2026d). We keep one prompt per unique question and do not place the released teacher responses in the policy input. Training and BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2025b) evaluation use closed-corpus retrieval. BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025), GAIA (Mialon et al., 2024), and xbench-DeepSearch (Chen et al., 2025a) use the same search, open, and find tools with Serper backend. Evaluation benchmarks. Final evaluation covers all 830 BrowseComp-Plus test questions, 1,266 BrowseComp test questions, 103 text-only questions from the GAIA development split, and 100 xbench-DeepSearch test questions. To limit temporal variation in live search, we interleave the open-web methods within the same evaluation window and archive the raw search responses with each generation. Reward function. The training reward is exact match, with 0.1 bonus for well-formed final-answer span. Table 1 reports exact match without that bonus. No evaluation question from either setting is used for policy optimization. E.2 Models The main experiments use Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 (Yang et al., 2025a). Appendix D.1 also trains Qwen3-1.7B and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) evaluates the corresponding initialization in the same agent interface. The model repositories are: 25 Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507. Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507. Qwen3-1.7B: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct: https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. E.3 Training and evaluation settings Optimization and systems. All runs use bfloat16 and SGLang on one eight-GPU node. Qwen3-4B uses FSDP. Qwen3-30B-A3B uses FSDP for Multi-Hop QA and FSDP2 for Deep Research, with rollout tensor parallelism of four on 96GB H20 GPUs. We train for 100 policy updates with AdamW, constant learning rate of 106, and weight decay 0.01. The Adam coefficients are (0.9, 0.999) for Multi-Hop QA and (0.9, 0.98) for Deep Research. We use no auxiliary KL penalty or entropy regularization, and sample training rollouts with temperature 1.0 and top-𝑝 1.0. Appendix D.4 repeats the Qwen3-4B comparison with five training seeds. TreeOPSD uses 𝑀 = 4, 𝑁 = 2, likelihood-weighted backup, target radius 𝜌 = 0.25, and 𝐸 = 4 sequential Forward-KL optimizer blocks, with unique-turn reconstruction. Task-speciﬁc settings. For Multi-Hop QA, collection uses 256 prompts split into four optimizer blocks of 64. Prompt and response lengths are capped at 2,048 and 6,144 tokens, retrieved observations at 16,384 characters, and each rollout at five assistant turns including the answer. Evaluation decodes one answer per question every five updates with temperature 0.6 and top-𝑝 0.95. For Deep Research, collection uses 128 prompts split into four blocks of 32, with prompt, response, and tool-observation limits of 4,096, 16,384, and 2,048 tokens. Training allows 60 assistant turns. BrowseComp-Plus evaluation allows 80 and greedily decodes one trajectory per question every five updates. Evaluation and checkpoint selection. We evaluate every five policy updates through step 80 on Multi-Hop QA and step 70 on BrowseComp-Plus, and report one checkpoint per run in that window. In Figure 8, the serialized trajectory stores two chat entries per assistant decision, so we divide both evaluation and training turn counts by two. The training-turn curve averages the rollouts collected at each checkpoint. Final Deep Research evaluation uses that checkpoint with one rollout per question, exact match against the short reference, at most 200 assistant turns, and 131,072-token response budget. The reported average weights the four datasets equally. E.4 Baselines and rollout-budget control Controlled methods. ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) evaluates the shared initialization without parameter updates. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) standardizes terminal rewards over complete rollouts from each prompt. GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025b) replaces token-level importance ratios with sequence-level ratio while retaining group-relative terminal advantages. TreePO uses the same initialize-then-expand trees, likelihood-weighted credits 𝑉𝑖, unique-turn reconstruction, prompt normalization, and optimizer blocks as TreeOPSD, but applies the fixed ascent coefficient 𝑉𝑖/𝐿 𝑥 throughout optimization instead of matching finite posterior target. Every trainable method applies four actor optimizer blocks per collected prompt batch. Rollout budget. GRPO and GSPO use 𝐺 = 8 rollouts per prompt. TreePO and TreeOPSD begin with 𝑀 = 4 complete trajectories, select 𝑁 = 2 branch-anchor occurrences from each, and sample one fresh terminal suffix per occurrence. Keeping the roots gives 𝑀 (𝑁 + 1) = 12 terminal leaves. continuation randomly starts from an intermediate prefix, so its expected generation length is roughly half that of root rollout, and the expected cost 𝑀 (1 + 𝑁/2) = 8 matches 𝐺. Appendix D.3 compares the methods at equal training time.

sections.title: F Data Examples
sections.content: This section shows one training record from each setting. We print the stored system message, the tool schemas injected by the Qwen3 chat template at rollout time, the stored user prompt, and the rule-based target. The serialized 26 RL row stores this chat prompt, the target, and per-example tool-routing metadata, but no teacher trajectory or hidden evidence. F.1 Multi-Hop QA (HotpotQA) The example is the first row of the HotpotQA distractor training parquet. The system turn is the stored system string with the chat-template tool block appended. The user turn is the Search-R1 instruction followed by the question. search call returns the top three passages from the fixed Wikipedia-2018 index with each query truncated at 512 characters. Multi-Hop QA (HotpotQA) Example System prompt: You are helpful and harmless assistant. # Tools You may call one or more functions to assist with the user query. You are provided with function signatures within <tools></tools> XML tags: <tools> { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "search", "description": "Searches the local wiki-18 dense retrieval index for passages relevant to the given queries.", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { "query_list": { "type": "array", "description": "A list of fully-formed natural-language search queries.", "items": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1, "maxLength": 512 }, "minItems": 1, "maxItems": } }, "required": ["query_list"], "additionalProperties": false }, "strict": true } } </tools> For each function call, return json object with function name and arguments within <tool_call></tool_call> XML tags: <tool_call> {"name": <function-name>, "arguments": <args-json-object>} </tool_call> Prompt: Answer the given question. You must conduct reasoning inside <think> and </think> first every time you get new information. After reasoning, if you find you lack some knowledge, you can call search engine. Emit one Hermes tool call per assistant turn and no surrounding prose in this form: 27 <tool_call> {"name":"search", "arguments":{"query_list":["fully formed search query"]}} </tool_call> The arguments value must be JSON object and query_list must be non-empty JSON array containing only non-empty strings. Never put bare query, Python syntax, Markdown fences, or trailing commas inside <tool_call>. The search engine will return the top searched results between <tool_response> and </tool_response>. You can search as many times as you want. If you find no further external knowledge needed, directly provide the answer inside <answer> and </answer>, without detailed illustrations. For example, <answer> Beijing </answer>. Question: Which magazine was started first Arthurs Magazine or First for Women? Ground-Truth Answer: Arthurs Magazine F.2 Deep Research (OpenResearcher) RL construction reads one OpenResearcher record per unique question and discards the teacher messages (Li et al., 2026d). All reported runs present only the question as the user turn, together with the system string below. The training row routes browser.search, browser.open, and browser.find to the fixed OpenResearcher corpus. Evaluation rows keep the same interface and select the fixed BrowseComp-Plus corpus or the Serper backend. Deep Research (OpenResearcher) Example System prompt: You are helpful assistant and harmless assistant. You will be able to use set of browsering tools to answer user queries. Tool for browsing. The cursor appears in brackets before each browsing display: [{cursor}]. Cite information from the tool using the following format: [{cursor}L{line_start}(-L{line_end})?], for example: [6L9-L11] or [8L3]. Do not quote more than 10 words directly from the tool output. sources=web When you have enough evidence, output your final answer in the exact form <answer>YOUR_ANSWER</answer> on its own line. Only the concise answer string goes inside; no citations, no explanations, no extra text after </answer>. Example final line: # Tools You may call one or more functions to assist with the user query. You are provided with function signatures within <tools></tools> XML tags: <answer>Paris</answer> <tools> { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "browser.search", "description": "Searches for information related to query and displays top results with titles, URLs, and summaries.", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { "query": { "type": "string", "description": "The search query string." }, "topn": { "type": "integer", "description": "Number of results to display; default 10." } }, "required": ["query"] } } } { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "browser.open", "description": "Opens zero-based result id from the most recent browser.search and displays line-numbered viewport. Use the number inside [id title]; do not use the [cursor] page number or an line number as id.", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { "id": { "type": "integer", "description": "Zero-based result id shown inside [id title], not the leading line number or [cursor] page number. Default -1 reopens the current page." }, "loc": { "type": "integer", "description": "Starting line; default -1." }, "num_lines": { "type": "integer", "description": "Number of lines; default -1." } }, "required": [] } } } { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "browser.find", "description": "Finds exact case-insensitive matches in an opened page.", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { "pattern": { "type": "string", "description": "The exact text pattern to search for." }, "cursor": { "type": "integer", "description": "Page cursor; default -1 means the most recent page." } }, "required": ["pattern"] } 29 } } </tools> For each function call, return json object with function name and arguments within <tool_call></tool_call> XML tags: <tool_call> {"name": <function-name>, "arguments": <args-json-object>} </tool_call> Prompt: Determine if Neil Patrick Harris has narrated the audiobook version of Henry Huggins. Ground-Truth Answer: Yes, Neil Patrick Harris narrated the audiobook version of *The Henry Huggins Audio Collection*.
